nameStory: Blackhaw gets its name from the dark, almost black color of its ripe berries and its incredibly hard wood. The 'haw' part is an old English word for a small fruit or berry, shared with hawthorns. Early settlers found the wood so tough it was nearly impossible to cut, earning it the nickname 'stag bush' because it was as stubborn as a stag's antlers!
description: Blackhaw is a medium-sized shrub or small tree that typically grows 12-15 feet tall, though it can reach up to 30 feet in ideal conditions. It's a member of the vibrant viburnum family, sporting clusters of creamy white flowers in spring followed by dark blue-black berries. The plant has a somewhat open, irregular branching pattern and smooth, oval leaves that turn brilliant shades of red and purple in fall, making it a real showstopper in the autumn landscape.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to elliptical leaves, 2-4 inches long, with finely toothed edges that feel slightly rough to the touch. They're arranged in opposite pairs along the branches and have a smooth, somewhat glossy surface that catches the light.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of tiny, creamy white flowers bloom in late spring, each cluster 2-4 inches across. The flowers have a sweet, pleasant fragrance that attracts bees and butterflies from quite a distance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small berries start pink in summer, then ripen to deep blue-black by fall. They're about 1/3 inch long, oval-shaped, and contain a single large, flattened seed. The berries taste sweet but somewhat dry.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark is dark gray-brown with a distinctive blocky, alligator-skin pattern that's quite rough to the touch. Young branches are smooth and reddish-brown.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Often grows as a multi-stemmed large shrub or single-trunked small tree with an irregular, somewhat open crown. Branches tend to spread horizontally, giving it a layered appearance.

habitat: Blackhaw thrives in well-drained soils along woodland edges, rocky slopes, and old fields throughout New England, though it's more common in the southern portions of the region. It prefers sunny to partially shaded locations and is often found growing with dogwoods, maples, and oaks. You'll most likely spot it in areas where forest meets meadow, as it enjoys the bright light but benefits from some protection.

seasonality.spring: Creamy white flower clusters burst open in May, filling the air with their sweet fragrance and creating a spectacular display against the fresh green foliage.
seasonality.summer: The flowers fade to reveal developing berries that start out pink and gradually darken. The green leaves provide a lush backdrop during the hottest months.
seasonality.fall: This is blackhaw's moment to shine, with leaves turning brilliant reds, oranges, and purples while the berries ripen to their characteristic blue-black color.
seasonality.winter: The distinctive blocky bark pattern becomes very evident, and you might spot dried berry clusters still clinging to branches, along with the opposite branching pattern.

funFact: Blackhaw wood is so incredibly dense and hard that Native Americans used it to make digging sticks and tool handles that could outlast metal implements - some blackhaw artifacts found by archaeologists are still perfectly preserved after hundreds of years buried in the ground!
confusionNotes: Blackhaw is most easily confused with nannyberry, another viburnum that also has dark berries, but nannyberry leaves are much larger (3-5 inches) with more pronounced veining, and its berries are rounder rather than oval. Remember: blackhaw has smaller, more oval leaves and oval berries, while nannyberry has bigger leaves and round berries.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'blackhaw' can be confusing because it's not related to hawthorns at all, despite sharing the 'haw' suffix. This is simply because both plants produce small, dark berries that early settlers grouped together under the old English term 'haw.' Blackhaw belongs to the elder family, making it more closely related to elderberries than to hawthorns.
compareHints: Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries. Its leaves are smaller and more finely toothed than nannyberry's, and it lacks the distinctive maple-like leaf shape of mapleleaf viburnum. The combination of oval leaves, oval berries, and exceptionally hard wood makes blackhaw unique among its viburnum cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
